title: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853
summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853, a DC-9-31, collided mid-air with a Piper PA-28 near Fairland, Indiana on September 9, 1969. The DC-9 was on an instrument flight plan descending for approach to Indianapolis at 3,550 feet when it converged with the VFR Piper aircraft. The Piper was not equipped with a transponder and did not appear on radar. At a relative speed of 350 mph, the left wing of the Piper sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly. Both aircraft lost control and crashed, killing all 83 occupants on both aircraft.
probable_cause: The deficiencies in the collision avoidance capability of the Air Traffic Control system in a terminal area with mixed IFR and VFR traffic. The deficiencies included inadequacy of the see-and-avoid concept, technical limitations of radar in detecting all aircraft, and absence of Federal Aviation Regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic.

factors.evidence: The Piper aircraft was not equipped with a transponder and did not appear as a primary radar target on the radarscope (p. 6).
The two aircraft converged at a relative speed of 350 mph at 3,550 feet; the left wing of the PA-28 sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly (p. 6).
The FAA system lacked adequate regulations for separating mixed IFR and VFR traffic in terminal areas (p. 6).
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year (p. 6).

events.text: Allegheny 853 departs Cincinnati at 15:15 EDT on IFR flight plan via airway V-97, initially cleared to 10,000 feet.
Piper PA-28 student pilot departs Brookside Airpark on VFR flight plan with cruising altitude of 3,500 feet.
Allegheny 853 reaches cruising altitude and is cleared on airway V-97 northbound.
Piper and Allegheny flight paths converge as both aircraft proceed toward Indianapolis terminal area.
Allegheny 853 begins descent from cruise altitude; vectored toward Indianapolis approach control.
Indianapolis Approach Control instructs DC-9 to descend from 10,000 to 6,000 feet, then to 2,500 feet.
Both aircraft converge in terminal area; Piper not visible on radar due to lack of transponder.
DC-9 and Piper collide at 3,550 feet; Piper left wing shears DC-9 tail; both aircraft crash near Fairland.

recommendations.text: Establish minimum standards for radar reflectivity of small aircraft
Mandate effective scanning patterns and procedures training for aircrews

safety_changes: Radar reflectivity standards for small aircraft
Enhanced scanning procedures and collision avoidance training

notes: Summary and history of flight sections
Radar limitations and ATC system deficiencies central to cause
All occupants of both aircraft killed
